messages.subject: Need help with a weird bug
parts:
Hi,

While writing the testing framework for vectorizing binary functions, I've come across a weird issue that I haven't been able to figure out over the last few days. Specifically,

using std::vector;
using stan::math::var;

vector<double> valid_inputs.size();
valid_inputs.push_back(1.3);
valid_inputs.push_back(-2.6);
valid_inputs.push_back(0);
valid_inputs.push_back(-0.2);
vector<var> b(valid_inputs.size());

var a = 1.3;

for (size_t i = 0; i < valid_inputs.size(); ++i) {

  for (size_t j = 0; j < valid_inputs.size(); ++j) {

    b[j] = stan::math::pow(a, valid_inputs[j]);

  }

  stan::math::set_zero_all_adjoints();

  b[i].grad(); 

  std::cout << a.adj() << std::endl;

}


will print out:

1.40646

-1.01106

0

-0.145982


but if I flip the argument order in stan::math::pow to:


b[i] = stan::math::pow(valid_inputs[j], a);


it will print out:

nan

nan

nan

nan


This is weird because a.adj() for b[0] should be 0.369004. Indeed, if you don't store the results of stan::math::pow into a std::vector<var> and you just take the derivative after calling stan::math::pow, it returns the correct values. Plus, the rev tests for pow all work. 


I tried looking at the autodiff paper and the code for pow in rev mode, but it's weird that it fails in this particular way. So, I wanted to email to see if I could get some help on it after trying to understand it for the last few days.


Thanks.


Best,

Rayleigh

I forgot that you can't read minds or haven't been staring at the code for a few days :).

What I wanted to show in the code block was a stripped down version of the testing framework and binary vectorize code. So, let me comment one of the code block and hopefully clear things up:

using std::vector;
using stan::math::var;
// Input vector of values to test

vector<double> valid_inputs.size();
valid_inputs.push_back(1.3);
valid_inputs.push_back(-2.6);
valid_inputs.push_back(0);
valid_inputs.push_back(-0.2);

// Return vector for the binary vectorize code
vector<var> b(valid_inputs.size());
// Input var to test

var a = 1.3;

// Represents testing framework code
for (size_t i = 0; i < valid_inputs.size(); ++i) {

// Represents the testing framework's call to binary vectorize code 

  // for the case of var, vector<T>

for (size_t j = 0; j < valid_inputs.size(); ++j) {

    b[j] = stan::math::pow(a, valid_inputs[j]);

  }
// Tests that the derivatives work for the given var in the return vector

stan::math::set_zero_all_adjoints();

  b[i].grad(); 

  std::cout << a.adj() << std::endl;

}

If binary_foo is my binary vectorized function, then these are currently valid function signatures:

binary_foo(stan::math::var x, std::vector<T> y)
binary_foo(std::vector<T> x, stan::math::var y)
binary_foo(stan::math::var x, Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> y)
binary_foo(Eigen::Matrix<stan::math::var, int R, int C> x, stan::math::var y)

If x is std::vector<T>, y stan::math::var, fx the return vector, and binary_fun is the function to be vectorized, then the behavior is essentially

for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
  fx[i] = binary_fun(x[i], y)

Generalizing it to the other signatures, it seems like we might run into this issue with derivatives.

That's not general enough. Each argument should be allowed
to be any of

var, vector<var>, Matrix<var,1,-1>, Matrix<var,-1,1>,
double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
int, vector<int>

So that's 100 instantiations. It might make sense to do it
with the VectorView template expression.

By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
it all? I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives
anywhere in those cases.

- Bob

Those aren't the only legal signatures; I only gave the ones that I thought were relevant to my question.

My concern is that in live code, it seems that if one derivative is NaN, the whole return vector or matrix will return NaN for its derivative. Is this something to worry about?

On Fri, Apr 29, 2016 at 3:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
That's not general enough.  Each argument should be allowed
to be any of

  var,    vector<var>,    Matrix<var,1,-1>,    Matrix<var,-1,1>,
  double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
  int,    vector<int>

So that's 100 instantiations.  It might make sense to do it
with the VectorView template expression.

By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
it all?  I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives
anywhere in those cases.

- Bob

parts:
Not ideal, but no worries for Stan code that's not buggy.

If one of the actual parameter values is NaN or has
a NaN derivative, we're going to reject in all of our
algorithms.

- Bob

> Those aren't the only legal signatures; I only gave the ones that I thought were relevant to my question.

>
> var, vector<var>, Matrix<var,1,-1>, Matrix<var,-1,1>,
> double, vector<double>, Matrix<double,1,-1>, Matrix<double,-1,1>,
> int, vector<int>
>
> So that's 100 instantiations. It might make sense to do it
> with the VectorView template expression.
>
> By "this issue", you mean we still have to figure out how to test
> it all? I think you can just safely segregate the illegal inputs
> leading to NaN derivatives and simply not worry about derivatives

>
> - Bob

There's an easy way to fix this, which is by refining the adjoint
code to return 0 * NaN as 0, but the test is way to expensive to
insert into every adjoint update, so we leave it this way.

- Bob
